questions.stem: Molly, 18, is seen in general practice with fever, a worsening generalised headache, photophobia and a stiff neck. She is alert. You lie her flat on the couch to test for Kernig's sign and tell the examiner what you are doing. Which manoeuvre tests Kernig's sign correctly?
options: Passively flex her neck and watch for involuntary flexion of her hips and knees
Raise her leg with the knee straight and note the angle at which pain begins
Flex her hip and knee to 90 degrees, then try to straighten the knee
Ask her to turn her head side to side quickly and note if the headache worsens
questions.why: For Kernig's sign, flex the hip and knee to 90 degrees, then extend the knee. Pain or resistance in the back or hamstrings is positive, because stretching the lumbosacral roots pulls on the inflamed meninges. A negative sign does not exclude meningitis.
notes: This is Brudzinski's neck sign, a different sign of meningism.
This is the straight leg raise (Lasègue's test) for lumbosacral nerve root irritation, such as a disc prolapse, not Kernig's sign.
This is jolt accentuation of headache, a separate bedside test for meningism, not Kernig's sign.

questions.stem: Molly, 18, is in a general practice with fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia. Repeat observations: T 39.3 °C, HR 130, RR 26, BP 108/66, SpO2 97%, alert. She has no rash and no known allergies. An ambulance has been called via 000. What is the most appropriate next step while you wait?
options: Take two sets of blood cultures and leave the antibiotic for the ED to give
Give benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV or IM now and record the dose and time
Give oral amoxicillin 1 g now so that absorption begins before transfer
Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV now and leave the antibiotic for the ED to give
questions.why: Suspected meningococcal disease outside hospital needs a parenteral antibiotic straight away: benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV or IM (eTG adult dose), or ceftriaxone 2 g IV or IM. Do not delay it for cultures or transfer, and send the drug, dose and time with her.
notes: Blood cultures are taken only if they cause no delay. Holding the antibiotic until the ED is a dangerous delay in suspected meningococcal disease.
Oral antibiotics are absorbed unreliably, do not reach adequate CSF levels and have no role in suspected bacterial meningitis.
Dexamethasone is an add-on given with or before the first antibiotic dose in hospital. Giving it without the antibiotic leaves the infection untreated.

questions.stem: Molly, 18, had a lumbar puncture in the ED for suspected meningitis. Her CSF is turbid, with neutrophils 8500 x10^6/L, protein 1.1 g/L and glucose 1.2 mmol/L. Her paired serum glucose is 5.0 mmol/L (ratio 0.24). Which mechanism best explains her low CSF glucose?
options: Serum glucose falls in sepsis and the CSF passively equilibrates with it
Increased CSF production by the inflamed choroid plexus dilutes the glucose
Cytokines trigger local insulin release that drives glucose into neurons
Bacteria and neutrophils use up glucose, and its carrier transport into CSF fails
questions.why: Glucose normally enters the CSF by GLUT1-facilitated transport and sits at about 60% of serum. In bacterial meningitis, impaired transport plus glycolysis by neutrophils, bacteria and inflamed brain lowers it. A CSF:serum ratio below 0.4 points to a bacterial cause.
notes: Her serum glucose is normal at 5.0 mmol/L. The very low ratio of 0.24 shows the problem is in the CSF, not in the blood.
The high opening pressure in meningitis comes mainly from impaired CSF absorption and cerebral oedema, not from extra CSF production diluting glucose.
No insulin is made in the CNS that could explain this. The fall comes from consumption and impaired transport.

questions.stem: In the ED, Molly, 18, has a lumbar puncture lying on her side. The registrar finds the level by feeling for the line joining the highest points of the iliac crests, then inserts the needle at the L3/4 interspace. Why is this interspace a safe site in an adult?
options: The conus medullaris ends at about L1–L2, so only cauda equina roots lie below
The dural sac ends at about L3, so CSF pools in a large cistern at L3/4
The conus medullaris ends at about L4, so the needle passes just below its tip
The filum terminale ends at L3, so the sac below it holds no neural tissue
questions.why: In adults the spinal cord ends at about L1–L2. Below this the lumbar cistern holds only the floating cauda equina roots, which move away from the needle. The intercristal (Tuffier's) line crosses the L4 spinous process or L4/5, so L3/4 and L4/5 are both safe.
notes: The dural sac continues to about S2, not L3. The lumbar cistern runs from the conus down to S2.
The conus lies at L1–L2 in adults. A cord ending at L4 would make L3/4 dangerous.
The filum terminale runs to the coccyx, and the cauda equina roots fill the sac below the conus.
